utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-16-T, the Prosecutor versus Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, Drago Josipovic, Dragan Papic and Vladimir Santic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. Before we continue with witness Vrebac, I would like quickly to deal with two sort of housekeeping matters, namely the two pending motions from Defence counsel, one concerning Witness DD, you may remember, Witness DD, and the other one concerning Mr. Mirsad Omsarovic. I think Defence counsel will by now have received the Prosecutor's response concerning Mr. Omsarovic, and this response, I think, was filed yesterday in response to the Trial Chamber's decision of the 2nd of March, '99. In that response, the Prosecution discloses to the Defence an annex which has been designated as annexe 5, and contains potentially exculpatory information relating to Drago Josipovic. Now, this Trial Chamber considers that the Prosecution has now fulfilled its duty under Rule 68, namely the duty to disclose exculpatory information in this regard, and, therefore, the matter is at a close. With regards to Witness DD, the Prosecution filed yesterday a response, ex parte, in which it averred that it had in its position no further exculpatory information or evidence on this witness. The Trial Chamber believes this declaration of the Prosecution to be convincing and in good faith, and so this matter is likewise close. We may now continue with witness Vrebac, and I would call upon Counsel Slokovic-Glumac to continue her examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: ZDRAVKO VREBAC (RESUMED)

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, Mr. Vrebac. I should like to ask you to take a look at the photographs first, and to tell us which the houses are. May I ask the usher to hand the photographs to the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D98/2.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. Vrebac, could you tell us which house is on the first page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The house on the first page is the one belonging to Milutin Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: The house of Milutin Vidovic is located across your house -- opposite your house; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It is in the same row as my house, the same side of the road. We're on the same side of the road.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And what about the building opposite?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean the second photograph?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Yes, the second photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The second photographer shows Milutin's house. Opposite that house is Ljuban Santic's house, and below you can just see the entrance and part of the roof of my sister's house. My sister's name is Jelina. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: That house served as a shelter, did it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And what about your father's house? It is opposite that house, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. My father's house is opposite my sister's house, and you can just make out the contours of the roof. You can see a small section of the roof from the auxiliary building belonging to my father.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said in your testimony so far that you also took part in the work of the cultural and art society of the SPS. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What was that society renamed later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in the course of 1992, it came to be known as the Citizens' Cultural Art Society of Vitez, which for us members -- it took us a little time to adopt the new name, to get used to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What about the composition of the members after 1993, before the conflict broke out, when the society got its new name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the composition of the members did not change, just some of the professional structures in it changed. That is to say Lili, I don't know his surname, we used to call him Lili, he played the harmonica with the folklore group, and he wasn't able to come because of his professional duties in Zenica. Drago Kozomovic was another case in point, but we did co-operate closely with them and ask their advice on various matters from time to time, that sort thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: How many Muslims were members of that cultural and art society in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. I can't tell you the exact number because there were three groups. There was the first group, which were the players that had already had a lot of experience, then there was the second group which we used to help us out and to replace anybody if need be, and the third group which was just learning the basics of folklore and folklore dancing. So I can't really say, but I think that the ratio was 50/50, half Croats, half Muslims. There were some Serbs as well together with us. That is what it was like more or less.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Zoran Kupreskic and Mirjan Kupreskic were members of that society at that time, were they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were. They were members at that time. Zoran Kupreskic was the main choreographer in the cultural and art society. Mirjan saw to the musical part, and so did I, as well as Fahrudin Ahmic. We were in charge of music. So it was up to the four of us to -- we -- the four of us in the cultural and art society were the principal ones.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: At that time, between the two conflicts, did you have any rehearsals and performances?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, every second or third day, depending on how we could distribute the rehearsals in the course of the week and whose turn it was, which group was to have its rehearsals. We didn't have regular performances, but we did from time to time. For example, for UNPROFOR. We had performances for UNPROFOR, and to celebrate some events in Vitez and the surrounding area.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You said in your testimony before that you played professionally in a band or group of some kind. Was Mirjan Kupreskic with you? Did he play together with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did, and I can enumerate for you. For example, that band, the band we had, was composed of Mirjan Kupreskic; Zdravko Vrebac, that is to say, myself; Vlatko Kupreskic; Fahrudin Ahmic; Nedzad Barucija; sometimes Ivo Jandric; and Naib Mekic. It all depended on the requirements, the person that asked us to play for them, what they wanted.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Fahrudin Ahmic, Nedzad Barucija -- and who was the other one you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said Naib Mekic from Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Yes, Naib Mekic. Are they Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: After the first conflict, that is to say, in November and December, did you have normal performances? Did you have any performances?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did. For example, we performed at UNPROFOR. We played there together with the cultural and art society from Travnik, and that society was called Borac. There were weddings. We played at weddings. For example, Zoran Vidovic's wedding, we played there. I can't remember the exact date but it was in that period, before the New Year, at all events. So we had different kinds of guest appearances.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you perform on television, in a television programme for the new year in 1992-1993, that New Year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I remember, it was sometime in December, and as I say, it was before the New Year when this television programme was filmed so that it could be broadcast within the New Year's programme. This we did for the local Vitez television station owned by Pero Gudelj. He was a well-known man this Pero. We were all up there. I don't know whether you want me to enumerate, the Muslims, the Serbs, the Croats, who were there. That was quite normal at that time. It was nothing strange that we were all there together.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: After the New Year, you had two other performances, one for the Muslim festival Bajram and one for Easter and Mali Mosunj. Did you attend both of these performances?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I attended the first performance, the Bajram celebration which was held at the fire brigade building in Old Vitez, and it was in the locality called the Mahala. That was a big celebration, a big festivity, and all of us were there. Anybody who had ever taken part in the cultural life of the region, which means that there were many members of the intelligentsia, and I think that there is a recording of that. It was a very nice celebration.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Were Zoran and Mirjan together with you there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. As I've already said, all the members of our cultural and art society took part in the performance on that occasion, everybody who worked for it, because it was at the municipal level, at the level of the town of Vitez, and it was a very large festivity, a major ceremony.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What about in Mali Mosunj for Easter? Did you have a performance with all the members there, and were you part of that performance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was. In Mali Mosunj, we performed for Easter, and the group was once again in full composition. That is, we had the whole orchestra with all its members. The folklore group had all its members taking part, all the dancers, just as we had done for the Bajram performance. This was how we worked. We would always give the best we could. Always for our audience we would give an all-out performance.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: After that performance, did you go anywhere? Did you go off anywhere, continue the celebration somewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. After that performance, we went on together, the whole of our folklore and art society, the folklore music group. We went to my own cafe in Vitez, and we stayed there until about 4.00 or 5.00, and then we went on. As I had a car, we went to Fahrudin Ahmic's so that he could say hello to his wife, say where he was, and then we went off to Mirjan Kupreskic's house where we stayed until late at night. We sat around talking about different things. In fact, we continued the festivity.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Were Muslims with you on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you know whether for Bajram, you would also go visiting the Muslim houses? Did Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic and the Croats go to congratulate the Muslims on their Bajram festivity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. And that was -- usually it was standard practice in our environment, because Vitez, as a town, was a multi-ethnic community, and there really was not any discord. We always supported each other. I can guarantee that. By all that is holy in the world, I can guarantee that. For Bajram, quite naturally, we went to Fahrudin Ahmic's once again, that is to say, Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan and myself. I don't remember who else. I think Zoran's family perhaps was there on that occasion. I'm not quite sure. Perhaps I mix up the visits we made because we went visiting very frequently. We would go to them. They would come to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Was it usual for the New Year to be celebrated together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. However, at that time, the hotels were not working, and so many of the larger premises for this kind of celebration, the buildings were taken over by UNPROFOR. For example, Tisa, the Tisa building in Busovaca, and other buildings and premises, for example, in Kiseljak. So there wasn't the space and the necessary halls to have an orchestra performing in the way that we were accustomed to. So on that particular year we would have these celebrations privately, in private houses. Mirjan and Zoran went to Mirko Vidovic to celebrate at their house, together with Naib Mekic and the neighbours. I went to see them there. I came in either before 12.00 or after midnight, I'm not quite sure, because on that particular evening I had -- as I am an electronics expert and I work in maintenance, I went to look at the equipment at Television Vitez, which was owned by Pero Gudelj, as I said. So I went up there and did part of my work. I serviced a piece of equipment, in fact, the equipment that was to show our television programme when we were at the television station, to record our musical programme.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You mentioned Naib Mekic, who also saw the New Year in with Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic and who was also a member of the cultural and arts society. Where did he live at the time? Do you happen to know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He lived in Kacuni, in his father's house there, and that is on the road between Busovaca and Kiseljak. Not far from the road. I can't explain, quite.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I'm just asking you the locality. Do you know whether Mirjan Kupreskic tried after the war to contact him and how he did this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in 1994 -- I don't know when, exactly. Maybe it was in May or June -- we went -- Mirjan Kupreskic and I, that is -- we went to the point at Kacuni which separated the Croatian from the Muslim part. We went there and we told the police on the Muslim side, if possible, to call Naib Mekic to come up, because it's not far from there, perhaps one kilometre or so to his house. They did. They went to call him, and Naib came. I cannot describe to you that meeting. We hadn't seen each other for such a long time, and we were all pleased to see each other. He was pleased to see us and we were pleased to see him, at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: How long had you not seen Naib Mekic? How long was he not able to go to Vitez and you were not able to go to Kacuni?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we saw each other -- the last occasion was prior to the conflict, several days before the second conflict broke out. Perhaps a few days before that. I think that we even had a rehearsal or were going to have a rehearsal, but I know that we saw each other at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What was the name of Fahrudin Ahmic's wife?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We called her Sutka. I think her real name is Suada. Yeah, Suada, Suada Ahmic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you know whether Suada Ahmic was in contact with Mirjan Kupreskic since the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. She did have contact with him. I don't know where they saw each other. I think they were in touch over the telephone. Since Mirjan realised that he was in a very, very difficult financial and material situation -- he told all of us about this, all of us from the cultural and arts society. Then we managed somehow, because we were not in a much better position. We managed to get a few things and some money, so that she would at least have something for the children. We all knew her and her children, and especially we did this for the sake of the late Fahran, and of course for the sake of the children, of course. We did that for him and another member of our society. His last name is Dzidic. I hope you won't mind, but we just know him by his nickname, Dzida, and I really can't remember his first name.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Perhaps Ahmed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dzida possibly. Possibly. Honestly, I cannot tell you exactly. If I had a picture of his -- I could show you exactly who the man is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What happened to Dzidic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he was also in that kind of a difficult material situation, and then he came to ask for help from those whom he believed would want to help him. So it wasn't a question of whether they would want to, but simply whether they could. Naturally he came to see Mirjan. This was 1994. Mirjan worked in Vitez, again, in the company Sutra, and he gave him -- of course, with the permission of his director, he gave him some more assistance in a material sense.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: The assistance that was given to Suad Ahmic; what year was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is also 1994. That is to say at the time of the checkpoints and everything, when she couldn't even come to see us. She didn't even have the money for the bus fare.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You said that before the war, Mirjan Kupreskic worked for a certain period of time in ^ Relaprovljak, in Ahmici, and after that at the retail in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Where did he work after the war, in '94, '95, and '96?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the war, I think this was April or May. I cannot say for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Which year is this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 1994. They started working with this warehouse and the shop in Vitez. Mirjan worked in Vitez, '94, '95, '96, until he came here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You know that he was employed at that time, and you saw him at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did. Well, let me just say another thing: He was not only employed, he was overemployed. He was way too busy. The entire company ^ Pepe Sutra was on his shoulders. He did everything. He was a manual worker. He was a bookkeeper.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: During that period of time after the war, did you leave the country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, we went to Switzerland. May I just have a look at something?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: No, it's not necessary, just tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What did you want to see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wanted to have a look at my passport. I want to see the date of issue because the date of issue is actually the date when we departed for Switzerland, and you can see it in the passport which day this was. We went there on a visit, the entire cultural and arts society went, and of course now, since this was after the conflict, it was without the Muslim part of the cultural and arts society, but again, I can say that there were Muslims who remained there, and I must say that some of them were very good dancers. We were in Zug in Switzerland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You said this was 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Just one more question. When you talked about the time between the two conflicts, and Mirjan's and Zoran's efforts in the cultural and arts society --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: -- their professional efforts, they played their instruments, et cetera. Also the fact that both of them had jobs at the time. I also have to ask you whether Zoran had a job at the time too?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, he worked in the SPS. I'm not sure. You see, at that time, it was not really compulsory, but it was customary to go on leave, and this leave what go on for five days or five months. He was certainly one of the best people that the company had, that that part of the company had, and I think that he worked all the time, practically. Often we would meet after work. I remember that distinctly. In '92, we would meet after work and all the way up to'93, we would meet at the cafe of the cultural and arts society that was owned by Sedzad, one of the members of the cultural and arts society.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: In view of these activities of theirs and their job and all the work they had, do you know whether they were part of the village guard or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think -- I don't know if I can really assess this. I don't know for sure, but I think, I think they were upset because we were often absent, and people were upset about that, you know, like, why would he guard your backyard from thieves? We were often absent in the evening. For example, we would play in Turbe until the very eve of the conflict with the Serbs in that part, and I remember that it was very difficult for us to get our instruments out and we played out there every evening in the restaurant centre which was to say that our neighbours were kind of upset that they were guarding our houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I have concluded, but I would just like to tender into evidence D97/2 and D98/2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No objection? Yes. So they are admitted into evidence. Counsel Pavkovic, is there any cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. No, the other attorneys are not going to examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Blaxill?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Vrebac, good morning to you, sir. My name is Michael Blaxill. I am one of the prosecuting lawyers in this case, and as a result of your testimony, I would like to ask you a number of questions, sir. Starting with, I believe you lived close to a gentleman by the name of Mr. Ivo Vidovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I believe he was a cafe proprietor and had a cafe near your home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: He was also, I believe, a member of the village guard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you ever perform village guard duties with Mr. Ivo Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Possibly, but we would see each other in cafes more often because that's the way we took this guard duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Well, that was going to be my next question: Did you frequent his cafe as a customer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I had the time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you have anybody in particular who assumed a kind of authority to coordinate and organise the village guard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No. No, no one special.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you, sir, know a man by the name of Mr. Nenad Santic? I hope I pronounced that correctly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you pronounced it correctly, and yes, I did know him. Although there was a generation gap between us. So yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Do you know whether Mr. Nenad Santic had any particular position or role with the HVO or in connection with running any kind of village guards or other organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think so. I think he was one of the first supporters of the HDZ in our community, but whether he had any special military or political significance, that, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: If I could take you forward even to the time after, say, the first conflict, when the conflict had actually broken out: Do you recall if Mr. Nenad Santic, at that time, assumed any kind of military or quasi-military role?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think so. Nothing more than any one of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Would it come as a surprise to you if I said that Mr. Ivo Vidovic stated that on the morning, indeed, of the second conflict, he received orders from Nenad Santic which he then obeyed? Would you find that a surprise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would. It would be a surprise for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I believe you generally, as a village guard, would patrol very close to your own homes, so within a village, the patrols would be very local to the particular residences of the members of the guard. Would that be so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, we mostly patrolled that part of the village by the neighbouring houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Would you say particularly after the separation of the guards, when the Muslims patrolled and the Croats patrolled separately, did you stay very much close to home in your performance of your guard duties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, after the second conflict, from time to time, we were in patrols together. For example, I, Mehmed Podojak, Islam Ahmic, Hadzija -- a neighbour of mine down the road, everybody called him Hadzija. I don't know his real name.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I'd like to take you back in time, if I may, to prior to the first conflict or between, let us say, the first and second conflicts: Is it not true that you performed those duties as individual guards of Croats and of Muslims and that you performed those duties close to your homes? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, nearby, that is to say in that neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vrebac. On the 20th of October you have stated you were awoken by an explosion at about 5.00 in the morning; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You stated that you then went to Zume, straightaway; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not immediately. Not immediately. After some time, when I got dressed, and I stayed there a bit. I don't know, perhaps around 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Around 6.00. Thank you. I believe you stated you went to the house of Mr. Ivica Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not into the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: But to the house --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I simply passed that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: -- the vicinity of the house. Just to clarify for my own understanding, if you would, sir, Mr. Ivica Vidovic and Mr. Ivo Vidovic: They are different people, or they are the same person, just different usage of the name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, these are two persons. Ivo Vidovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you. I just wanted that clarified. I'm grateful to you. When did you find out about the cause of that conflict on the 20th of October, namely being the Muslim barricade or checkpoint that had been erected on the main road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I found out about the cause that day, but I found out a day earlier that the roadblock had been set up, although we didn't really think this would be a special problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So in fact you knew about the existence of this on the previous day. So when you awoke on the morning of the 20th of October, can you tell us what immediately crossed your mind, having heard that explosion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My first thought -- well, I really didn't think about anything. I was only afraid when I heard that detonation. Afterwards, perhaps, I did connect this with the erection of the roadblock. But again, I didn't know for sure what was going on, or the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: At that time, after that explosion, I believe you stated you heard shooting coming from the direction of the Catholic cemetery; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but not immediately. Not immediately after the explosion, but perhaps around 6.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And by 6.30, where were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I told you a few minutes ago that I got dressed and I went to Zume. I saw this around 6.00. That is to say, I was passing by Ivica Vidovic's house, and I went to this place where there is a natural depression, and around 6.30 this shooting started.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Had you taken a weapon with you when you left your home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I took my M-48 rifle. Its popular name was Tundzara. I already explained what the purpose of this rifle was and who it was owned by.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So by 06.30 that morning of October 1992, you had reached that area of depressed land which I believe is not far from the house of Mirko Sakic; is that right, roughly speaking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No. About 30 to 50 metres away, in that area. That is to say, between the house of Niko Sakic and below Ivo Kupreskic's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you. At that time then, at about 06.30, you started hearing shooting; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You say that shooting was coming from the direction of the Catholic cemetery?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: How far away from you was the Catholic cemetery at that time? From where you were to the Catholic cemetery, how far?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can tell, about 800 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: About 800 metres. You have given this court a description that from where you were, you described a hail of bullets, that there are bullets flying thick and fast in the area where you were. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't mention a hail of bullets in that area, I said that when we went to pick up Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic's family, that is to say, in that area, between their houses and Ivo Kupreskic's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: From the depression where you say you were at that time, how far was it to the houses of Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About a hundred metres, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So you say that 100 metres away from you, by those houses, you say there was a hail of bullets, the bullets were flying thick and fast. Is that now correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No, no, this is not accurate. I said that at the moment when we were going to carry the children of these people, these bullets were flying above our heads. That is to say, in that area. That is to say, we had already picked up the children. That is to say, when the shooting had already started, after 6.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: How far was it from the houses of Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic to the area of the Catholic cemetery where the fighting was going on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I don't have a very good sense of distance, but perhaps about 700 or 800 metres, roughly speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So, in point of fact, it would appear, from what you're saying, that when you went to collect those children there were lots of bullets flying around you that emanated from a conflict taking place over half a kilometre -- three-quarters of a kilometre away from you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, when you went to the houses of Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic, could you tell me what time that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, just after the shooting started. I don't know how much time would have gone by. Perhaps only five minutes, because we were afraid, because their families were in the houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So let us say it was sometime shortly after half past six in the morning. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Is it correct that there were shelters at the houses of either Mirko Sakic or one of the Vidovic houses close to that depression where you had been? There were shelters there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Shelters were in the garage of Niko Sakic, and as one goes from Sakic's house to my house is the house of Niko Vidovic, son of Juko, because there are three Niko Vidovic's in Zume. So this is very important to highlight this. Yes, there were these shelters.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Presumably from what you've said about the distances, these shelters would be within a hundred to a hundred and fifty-odd metres from the houses of Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic. Would that be about right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would be correct in terms of Sakic's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: To be precise, we will say that the first available shelter would have been at about that distance, is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, you, in fact, with Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic, you said that you took their families all the way down to nearby where you live, the house of your sister; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Can you tell me, sir, why you, with all these bullets flying around at that time, as you say, why you did not try and seek shelter in the first available safe shelter to be had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, let me repeat. These bullets were flying around in the area. We had to pass from their house to Ivo Kupreskic's house. Further on there was no danger to us. The reason why we went up to the shelter to my sister's house, was quite simply a question of space, how many people could be accommodated into a certain premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you check the other shelters before moving on down to your sister's house to see how many people were in there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At Niko Sakic's there were a lot of people there. There were people from neighbouring houses, and the space is small, so it was a restricted space. Niko Vidovic's house, Juka's, we didn't go to because -- let me explain something to you. Each of us had a place they liked to go to and a place they didn't like to go to, so we would choose places where we would rather go, and so that was probably what they felt in my house, that is to say, my sister's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So are you saying that, in fact, it was a matter of personal choice, not just a matter of space?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Space is the first thing we considered, and of course, everybody has the right to choose where he wants to go. The safety of the premises at my sister's house was not brought into question because it was the firmest built house in the locality.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you. I will, however, ask you just one question again, and you may answer if you will, sir, with just a "Yes" or a "No". Did you personally check as to any available space in the shelters at Mirko Sakic or Niko Vidovic's houses? Did you check yourself or did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At Niko Sakic's, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, after you went down to your sister's house and the families of Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic were delivered into safety, what did you then do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We then returned to the depression. We then had put the children in safety and we went back to the depression.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Were Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic with you in that depression at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The entire time we were together, from the morning, from about 6.30, till the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Were all of you armed during that period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: -- weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I remember, only myself and Mirko Sakic had weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I think you've referred to the depression as being an area that was to be commonly used as an area to shelter the population in a time of potential danger, but did you have any -- as village guards, did you have any kind of instructions or even understanding of any kind of guard duty you would be performing by being in that location?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. There was no guard duty going on there. I would rather put it through a sort of instinct. Instinctively. I don't know how to put it. Probably you can see from the map, if you can see the depression on it. The hill divides -- above the depression divides Ahmici, and the depression, that hill is like a two-storey building, which means it is six to seven metres high, and it instils a feeling of safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So what you're saying, sir, I believe, is that the depression itself gives -- about six to seven metres deep; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, according to my assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Very well. How many people sort of turned up at the depression, rather like yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, with us, there was Mirjan, Zoran Kupreskic, myself, Mirko Sakic, Milutin Vidovic, Dragan Vidovic, Nikica's son Ivica Kupreskic, Niko Sakic, Drago Grgic, Dragan Samija, Mirko Grgic, and Anto Brnada.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You're saying to us, sir, that there was no pre-arrangement or instructions regarding people turning up at this depression; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there wasn't. I mentioned a moment ago the instinct that guided us. We were like bees, behaving like bees. It was warmer there. That is to say, we felt safer being together there. We felt lost, and if we were altogether we found it easier to bear.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Very well. So you're saying essentially that the fair number of people that you have named all essentially must have shared an instinct to go directly to that place; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. When I say instinct, I don't say a natural instinct. I mean something that has been learnt from previously. I said why that particular spot was so interesting. In the former Yugoslavia was it designated as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I believe, sir, the firing ceased at something like 16.00 hours, 4.00 in the afternoon; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, around 3.00 or 4.00. I can't tell you the exact time, because, first of all, there would be a lull, first of all, and then about 4.00 it ended completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Up to that time of 4.00, had you caught sight at all of Mr. Ivica Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ivica, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Whereabouts had you seen him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I first saw him in the morning. That is to say, when the shooting started. I saw him in front of his house when we peaked through to see what was happening. I saw him, and Mirjan and Zoran when we went to fetch the children. Then he moved away, because his house is up on the hill. It is exposed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you by chance see a Mr. Vlatko Kupreskic at all during that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I think that Vlatko was in his own house, that he didn't go anywhere. That's my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I believe the house of Mr. Vlatko Kupreskic is very close to that of Mr. Zoran and Mr. Mirjan Kupreskic, the houses of Mr. Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, if we may, sir, move on. After the first conflict on the 20th of October, it seems that the Muslims who had left town came back about three to four days later. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thereabouts, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Prior to that there had been a meeting or meetings to try and resolve some terms whereby they would feel reassured and return to the village of Ahmici; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know whether they agreed on terms. I think they agreed on just the way in which people could be convinced to go back, because of course, all the people were terrified.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Do you have any idea of what ways were agreed? Do you have any idea of what matters were settled to achieve this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know the details, but it was agreed that a trust be returned, because the people were afraid of the conflict, and they wanted to try to convince them to go back to find a formula for this. There was no other way but just for them to try to go back. This was what was done in the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge of who attended the meeting or meetings that resulted in this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to what my father said and as far as I'm able to remember the story that was told afterwards by my father, I think that some of the head people from the Croatian part of the municipality were there, Ivica Santic and Pero Skopljak, I think. Some of those prominent individuals from the world of politics. Whereas on the Muslim side, I think that there was Sefkjia Dzidic, and Berbic, I think. I'm not quite sure, because I don't know those people very well either.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: To your knowledge, were any of the local people involved, local Croats or Muslims from Ahmici and surrounds?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, all the elderly and prominent individuals, people who had more understanding for things like that. That is to say, people who had more experience through life, quite simply, to put it in simple terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Do you recall if any members of the Kupreskic family were involved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My father told me, yes, that Anto Kupreskic was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Were you aware of any involvement of Mr. Zoran Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know because I heard about it. That is to say, my father told me. Niko Sakic -- there were quite a number of people there. Zoran Kupreskic enjoyed, at the time, great respect in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you stated that obviously the Muslims returned and a relative calm returned to the area of Ahmici; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: However, would it be true to say that the tensions between the ethnic communities still remained somewhat high? There were tensions in the air; was that not so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that there were tensions, that's my opinion, but not with all the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, if I understood your evidence correctly, sir, you stated that there were a number of further alarms or alerts that occurred in the months between the first conflict, in October '92, and the one in April 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Can you tell me on how many occasions you recall there being an alert?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I can't remember. Two or three times, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Maybe two or three times. On those occasions, do you recall anybody taking to the shelters in and around Zume and Ahmici, Pirici, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, it was a normal reaction on the part of the ordinary people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: On those two or three occasions, do you recall, what did you do in response to the alarm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to the warehouse because there wasn't a guard there all the time, but we would take turns, take shifts, when we could, when we had some free time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So on each of those occasions, you went to your warehouse?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For the most part, yes. Sometimes I didn't even go home because I wasn't married at the time. I was a bachelor. So I went around. I got around. But mostly I would go to the warehouse, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Because you have told this Chamber that, on the 20th of October, you followed an immediate instinct to go across to the depression in response to an alarm, and yet you're saying that subsequently when there were alarms your response was very different; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, there's a difference between night and day. It's different when you're thinking about it. You think differently during the night and day. My duties vis-à-vis the warehouse, particularly as my brother was taken prisoner during the first conflict, at Opara, and I didn't have anything to do in the warehouse because it wasn't open.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: What time of day or night were these other alarms that you recall then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't say exactly. Generally, during the night, when people are most afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Let's move on, if we may, sir, to April of 1993 -- oh, no, I'm sorry, I have one further question, if I may, in respect of the first conflict. You heard the sounds of shooting and so forth. You have not mentioned hearing any other kinds of sounds. You heard no broadcasts or anything of that nature in the course of that day, broadcast of voices in any way, in October?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I just heard from my father's stories.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: But you certainly, then, heard nothing by way of any kind of message or voice being broadcast over loudspeakers during the warning of October the 20th? Just to be sure about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was woken up by detonation. What my father told me, according to what he said, that had happened before the detonation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, if we may now move forward, as I've said, to the 15th of April. You were now at that point running a cafe in Vitez; that's correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You say it was a perfectly normal day for you, normal business?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, quite normal. Like any other day. Children were going to school. Why wouldn't it have been a normal day?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did anything become a kind of hot item of conversation, you know, an important item of conversation with your customers, in the course of that day? Any particular piece of news?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not that day. We didn't get any special information about anything going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So on the 15th of April, 1993, you didn't hear, then, about the apparent kidnapping of a Croat military commander by the name of Mr. Totic that occurred in Zenica that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That day I heard this when I came home at about 8.00 p.m. or 9.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, considering your return home, you've said about 8.00 or 9.00 p.m. Where did you go initially when you came back from Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I came back from Vitez, I've already said that we stayed with our relatives for a little time above the warehouse at Slavko Vrebac's. That's where we stayed. We sat around there for a little time. Iva and Marijan were there. They're my generation, so we had a lot to talk about, so we sat around and chatted for some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you, at any time that evening, call by on Mr. Ivica Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So from the house you have mentioned, of Mr. Slavko Vrebac, you then went to your own home; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You were woken up at about half past 5.00 in the morning, I believe -- I'm sorry, no, at 5.00 in the morning of the 16th -- by your father?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, my father woke me up at about 5.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: On this occasion, at that time there was no firing going on or anything like that, at 5.00; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: On this occasion, you responded, it seems, as you had with the other previous alarms in '93, and you went to your warehouse; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Just to confirm the times that I've observed from -- this was probably about -- what, about 6.15 you arrived at the warehouse, or shortly after 6.00, and you noticed smoke, pillars of smoke over Ahmici by about 06.15, 06.30; is that about right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that's not the way I put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Are those timings accurate, or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, look. The shooting started about 5.30 in the morning. At that time, I was already in the warehouse, and I was already with a guard who had been there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I'm just trying to check that I have noted the times correctly, sir. I believe it was between 06.00 and 06.15 you and the guard noticed the smoke over Ahmici; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, approximately at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: At about 06.30, you telephoned your brother in Split?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, do you recall, when your father woke you, any information he gave you as to who had alerted him or how he came to know there was a problem or an alarm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was awakened by the people who came to the shelter. They were from Krtine Mahala, from that area. They came to ask him for the keys so that they could get in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I see. Thank you. So that's what alerted your father. He in turn woke you up. Thank you, sir. Now, you then came back from the warehouse and brought some food to the shelter; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Can you tell me roughly what time that was that you came back down to the shelter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I can't say exactly what time it was. Between 9.00 and 10.00. Around 9.00, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: At 21.00. So we can make it absolutely clear that you had not seen Mirjan or Zoran Kupreskic up to this point of 9.00 on the morning of the 16th of April; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: When you got to the shelter, I presume, sir, that was the shelter at your sister's house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I believe you said it was at that point that you saw Mirjan and Zoran Kupreskic, on the morning of the 16th; is that correct, sir? Or have I made ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I took that food. I put it into the shelter. I gave it to the people. When I was leaving my sister's house, I saw them coming in front of the shelter so they could see Mirjan Kupreskic's family.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So you encountered them there. Did you or had you up to this point of the day seen Mr. Vlatko Kupreskic at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My father told me that he was there at the shelter, but I didn't see him because I didn't go down into the shelter itself, only into the hallway where the staircase is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So you personally did not have any encounter with Mr. Vlatko Kupreskic to that point on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Personally, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you see or did you have any kind of contact with Mr. Vlatko Kupreskic subsequent to 9.00? In other words, at any time during the rest of the 16th of April.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't know when after that, but not those days.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So after that visit to the shelter, you were there at about, you said, sometime after 9.00; what did you do from there? Where did you go from the shelter, having delivered the food?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as I said, we talked. Mirjan Kupreskic, Zoran, Mirko, and I, we talked about everything that was going on, and then we realised that our friend and a member of our orchestra was killed. What did we do? We cried, in response to all of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: How long do you think, sir, your conversation was with Zoran and Mirjan in the vicinity of the shelter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know. At that time, I don't see who could have measured time. But perhaps half an hour or 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Regarding the sad news of your friend being killed, who was it again who gave you that news?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was told by Mirjan, Zoran, and Mirko Sakic. They were told by Vidovic Anto, called Satko, who on that day, was with Fahrudin Ahmic's mother, and she had told him about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I don't know if the exhibit is still there, Your Honours. I'd like to refer briefly to D97/2, the last of the maps we've been using. I will say that is the only paper exhibit I have in the course of my cross-examination, Your Honours. There will be no more.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Vrebac, I would be grateful, sir, could you please point out the home of Mr. Fahrudin Ahmic on the map that is on the machine next to you? Would you just point to it with that device?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Over here in this part of the houses (indicating). I cannot exactly pinpoint the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Does the mother of your late friend live nearby to his house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She lived in the house right by the main road. That's where the mother and the father lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You heard that she had been encountered by Mr. Anto Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Sir, had Mr. Vidovic ever been to that part of the territory, if you like? Did you know that or were you told that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was told that, that he was with her in Ljuba Vidovic's house, or Alojzije Vidovic's house. I'm the not sure, but Ljuba Vidovic -- let me just show you that house.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes, if you would, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: It's down there. Is that close to, I believe, a place called the Pican cafe? Is that close to where you pointed to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pican's cafe.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Do you recall what time of day Mr. Anto Vidovic was supposed to have met this lady?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I don't know what time. I don't know about those details. I just know that he was with her.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You say you obviously received this news somewhere between 9.00 and 10.00 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, when you parted company with Mr. Mirjan and Mr. Zoran Kupreskic, again, can you estimate roughly what time that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said perhaps half an hour after our encounter, 40 minutes afterwards. I don't know. I think I -- I left there. I left my parents' place. I went from the shelter to the warehouse around 10.30, around 10.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Do you recall where Mr. Mirjan or Mr. Zoran Kupreskic went at that time? Did you see them going any particular direction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. They went in the direction of Milutin Vidovic's house, because that's where Zoran's family was. They went in that general direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Where did you go at that time, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to my parents to see whether they needed anything, and then I went straight to the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Zoran or Mr. Mirjan Kupreskic at any time during the rest of that day, the 16th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you have any form of contact with them, perhaps by telephone or anything like that, for the rest of that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I believe you stated in your evidence-in-chief here, sir, that on the second day of that event, the 17th of April, 1993, you did not see Zoran or Mirjan Kupreskic at all. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not on the second day, only on the third day we met.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes. I was going to say, sir, yes, the third day. You did, in fact, see Mr. Mirjan and Mr. Zoran Kupreskic. Can you just refresh my memory, sir, as to what time of the day you can say that you saw them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I already said, on the third day of the conflict, sometime around noon. That is to say, sometime around 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Where did you encounter them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not really encounter them. It would be more accurate to say that I went out looking for them. I went to find them to see what was going on, what was happening. I was curious. I found them behind Niko Sakic's house, in that same depression.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Can you recall what they were wearing at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zoran, I think, was only wearing a camouflage shirt, and it was much bigger than what he would need. Mirjan wore civilian clothes. I don't know exactly what they were like. I think he was wearing a brown jacket, but he was wearing civilian clothes, at any rate.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Were either of them armed with a weapon at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. They both had weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Can you describe for us, please, what weapon was in the possession of Mr. Mirjan Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had the same kind of rifle as I did, M-48, popularly called Tandzara.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: What weapon was in the possession of Mr. Zoran Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had a smaller gun, a smaller hunting gun. I'm not very knowledgeable as far as hunting guns are concerned. It was a carbine, if that's the right word.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, I believe you said that sometime on that day, I believe the third day, some HVO soldiers came and ordered you to go to Barin Gaj. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They came into an area between the warehouse and my uncle's house, and we were at my uncle's, that is to say, my other cousins and I, and that is when they took us down there below Barin Gaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: What is it precisely that you had to do there? Were you put into some kind of line, or dug into a trench or something like that? I wasn't quite clear from what you said as to what you had to do there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had to dig trenches, and we had to set up a defence line. That is to say, we were digging these trenches for ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You stated that then, I think, you had to spend 20 days, 20 further days at that location. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Approximately. I cannot say what the exact date was when I left that place. About 20 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Were you given time off at all during this duty? Could you go home to sleep at any time? Could you take a break and have some rest, or did you have to stay in that spot continually, 24 hours a day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you that I had a bit of a more privileged position there. The reason for that was that I actually -- I don't know whether this can be translated. I was actually in charge of the warehouse of the company of Trgogrozd, owned by my brother, and there was quite a bit of food over there, so I had to issue this food. I mean, I wanted to too, to give this food out for people who were in shelters, and these people who were on the line with me, et cetera. At the time when I went to get these supplies and to give them to them, I would also take a bath, get some sleep, et cetera, but I cannot say the same as for the others. They were there round the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, I think you said it was something like the fifteenth day after the initial conflict that you, in fact, drove Zoran and Mirjan's families into Vitez. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So logically and presumably, you were able to take time off from that line duty to be able to perform that favour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just told you now. The favour that was done at that time to Mirjan and Zoran was to let them leave the line to take care of this, because I said a few minutes ago that everybody was there 24 hours a day, and I already said that I had a bit of a privileged position.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So from this answer, you're saying that Mr. Mirjan and Zoran Kupreskic, they were in that line with you? That's how it appears in the transcript. I just want to clarify. Were they at Barin Gaj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not see them, and I did not know exactly where they were those days. They were certainly in that part of the line, but I cannot pinpoint the exact spot and I didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Right. So in other words, somehow, permission was arranged for all three of you to take the families into Vitez and leave the line to do so? That would seem to be so; yeah?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, after the first day of the conflict, the 16th of April, did you see Mr. Vlatko Kupreskic in subsequent days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did see him, but when, on what days, that I do not know. Quite a bit of time has gone by. I saw him somewhere in the area of Zume or somewhere around there, perhaps when I was going home, but when I was at the line, that is to say, sometime after that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I'd just appreciate a moment to confer with my colleagues if I may, Your Honour. Mr. Vrebac, thank you for answering my questions. Your Honours, that concludes the cross-examination. I'm obliged to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Blaxill. We will now take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Slokovic-Glumac?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. Vrebac, when you described the first conflict which took place in 1992, you said that there was shooting towards the Kupreskic houses.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you know where the shooting was coming from? Did you see the people who were shooting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't see the people, nor did I think of looking at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you, in that part of the village, see any soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: The bullets that you said were showering, hailing around the house, was it the shooting above the houses, below them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How do you mean above or below?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: How high was this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, perhaps it was 50 metres high up in the air, but at the time I thought it was just above my head, so I can't really assess the distance. You could see the sound of bullets whizzing past.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: The direction of the shooting, were you able to determine that or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean the direction from which the shooting was coming?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Yes, from which the shooting was coming.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the area of the cemetery, in that line, but it's difficult to determine, particularly not at that point. I could perhaps reconstruct it and do it that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So, in fact, you heard the bullets and you saw that bullets were flying around the house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I heard that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Tell us, at that point in time when you were pulling out the children, were the people who were there, the Kupreskics and the children, and those of you who had come to take the children away, were you afraid?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, very much afraid. I would say more for the safety of the children that we were taking with us, because there were two babies. They were up to the age of one. There was little Marko -- and we were afraid for the children, and, of course, for our own safety as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You said that the shooting was in the area between the houses of Mirjan Kupreskic and his father, and Ivo Kupreskic. Have I understood that correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: This part of Zume, where you passed through, was there any shooting there at all? Could you hear bullets flying by, anything like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there was no shooting there, although we could hear -- that is to say, there was the ugly sound of a bullet. I don't know where it could have been fired from, but you could always hear the shooting coming from one spot, and that is the area of the cemetery, from that particular locality.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: On that day, did you know what was going to happen later on and how the conflict would expand, whether it would expand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. We knew nothing at all, nothing about the conflict or the cause of the conflict. We were not certain whether the cause was the barricade or not, or whether it would expand towards us. I don't know. We were quite simply, totally uninformed, and we weren't terribly inquisitive either, to go around asking people. We just hid where we could and stayed there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Tell us, how many Croats live in Santici and Pirici? Could you give us an estimate, in those two parts of the village which are dominantly Croatian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't even give a rough estimate. I'm afraid that I'll give quite a wrong figure. I don't know. Let us say about one thousand, one and a half thousand -- I really don't know. I really can't say. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: The people that you enumerated having seen on the 20th around the house of Niko Sakic, and you named seven people, I believe -- seven to ten people, I don't know exactly -- tell us, what area were these people from? Where were their houses? We know about the Kupreskics. What about the rest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the houses of the others were close by, too, at a maximum distance of 300 metres from there. They were all from the surrounding houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did any of these people fire a single bullet on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No. None of those people fired, not at any event. They could not have. Only Mirko Sakic and myself could have fired because we had weapons. The others didn't even have weapons, so they couldn't have fired. It was quite beyond us, the thought of firing. We didn't think of it at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you on that day see any other Croat from Santici and Pirici who might have taken part in the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You also said that Zoran Kupreskic was greatly respected in the village. Tell us whether he was respected only among the Croats or among the Muslims as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. He was generally respected by the inhabitants of the region. He was very well educated, and he was, in principle, a good man, and that was why people respected him. I know that for a fact, and from what other people have said about him, both the Muslims and the Croats, regardless of ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: The second conflict, in April 1993, do you know when the people left the shelters? Do you know whether they got any information on the second day, of any kind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I heard of this in the morning, that is to say, they left on the evening of the second day in the direction of Rovna. However, I did not know at the time that anything was going on. In the morning, when I went to visit my parents, I saw that there was nobody in the shelters, nor were my parents in their house. That is when I realised that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you know what information was conveyed to the people in the shelters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they were told that the Muslim forces -- in concrete terms the Mujahedeen. That was what the information said -- that they had passed in the area of Recez Creek. It is below the Krtina-Mahala region and goes on up to the first houses in our own village.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Apart from the fact that the Croats from Pirici and Ahmici had left, do you know that people from Krtina-Mahala had left as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, people from Krtina-Mahala had also fled because that is the most exposed section of that area. If you look at the area as a whole, that is the most exposed region, the Muslim area, next to them. So they had left as well and went to Rovna.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did the Muslims really break through the line at Krtina-Mahala?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Afterwards, we learnt that the line had not been broken through, but that there was a strong attack on that portion that evening. Probably it was a reaction on the part of the people who were watching this from the rear, that they had seen some people's sheds set on fire and burning. So probably this was a disinformation, in fact, but it was always good to be wary.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Therefore, that information was not true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Tell us, you talked about the alarm and the alert. How was this alert sounded? Was there a siren, a sound signal, or were there couriers, or was there a third way in which the alarm or alert was sounded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, usually there was a sound alert from Vitez, from the police building, I think it was, or perhaps the PTT building, or the fire brigade building, but it was done by means of sound, a sound alert.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Was there any information conveyed in other ways apart from this ^ soundtrack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I don't know who could give out this information. The way in which we -- and I'm here thinking of my family, how we got to know about it -- was that the people came who were looking for shelter and wanted to be put up in the shelters. I can't really tell you anything else about that. I don't know, quite simply. I don't know who could have told them and informed them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. We have no questions for the witness. Mr. Vrebac, thank you for giving your testimony here. You may now be released. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Now, we now have a problem, because we have two more witnesses, and I wonder whether we could get through with at least one of them today. Do you think, Counsel Slokovic-Glumac, that the next one -- you don't have many questions for the next one? Because it would be very awkward, you know, to start the examination or cross-examination and then resume with the re-examination or cross-examination in one week's time. So if we could at least finish one. Do you think it's worth trying? Counsel Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, we're certainly not going to be able to get through two witnesses, and I think it will be difficult to get through one witness, as well.
