So I fear that one witness will be up for cross-examination, at least. If you feel that it would be better to round off the examination of each individual witness, then it would be a good idea to start the first witness another time so that we have the examination in chief and cross-examination at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Since we can't afford to waste time, I think we should maybe start with one witness and see whether we may able to finish with one. Thank you. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mrs. Kupreskic. Could you please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Counsel Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Kupreskic, can we start?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Kupreskic, could you please introduce yourself to the Court. Could you please tell the Court your date of birth, the day, month, and year, and also your maiden name?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I'm Ankica Kupreskic, born Grabovac. I was born in Vitez on the 15th of July, 1957. I'm a catering worker by profession, and I have three sons.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: And please tell us your current address?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Petar Svacic street, Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Before you got married, before you married Ivica Kupreskic, could you tell me where you lived?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I lived in the village of Krcevine, by Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: And when did you get married?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I got married on the 26th of February, 1978.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: After you got married, where did you go to live?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: After I got married, we left about seven months later. We went to Kruscica. That is also a suburb of Vitez, and that's where we lived for less than a year. We built a house and then we went back to our house.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Where is this house of yours?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: In the village of Pirici, by Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: How many children do you have?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I have three sons.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: When you came to live in Pirici, do you remember, in Pirici, who your neighbours were? First, list your Croat neighbours and then list your Muslim neighbours, please.

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Well, there was Mirjan Kupreskic; his father, Anto Kupreskic; my brother-in-law, Josip Kupreskic; my other brother-in-law, Branko Kupreskic; my husband's father, Ivo Kupreskic; and then the neighbour, Vidovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: All right. So those were Croats. Could you give us your Muslim neighbours now?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: The Muslim neighbours were Enver, Sulejman, Zulejha, Sakib --

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: You also have to give us their last names.

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know their last names, not all of them. It's Sakib Ahmic, Sulejman Pezer, Enver Sehic and Zulejha Ahmic. I think that was her last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please get up for a minute and look at this large aerial photograph of Ahmici? Try to find your own house, please, as well as the houses of your neighbours. Then on a smaller map, or rather on a smaller photograph, we're going to ask you to mark this. So first of all, please show your own house, and then show the houses of your Croat neighbours, and then show the houses of your Muslim neighbours. You won't be able to manage -- oh, you will. Oh, it's a long wire. When you show something, tell us what it is. All right. So start with your own house. Where was your house?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: This is my house (indicating). This is my house. This is my house. This is Josip's house, my brother-in-law (indicating). This is Zoran Kupreskic's house (indicating). This is the house of Mirjan Kupreskic's father (indicating). This is the warehouse of Vlatko Kupreskic. Up here is Enver's house, and Alaman's house, and up here, Sakib's house (indicating). This is the house of Vlatko Kupreskic (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: All right, please take a seat. Thank you. I would ask the usher now to hand out these aerial photographs, and then we're going to give a copy of this aerial photograph to the witness to put a circle around some of the houses that she spoke of.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document is (inaudible) /1 --

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Please take a marker now and put the photograph on the machine next to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: The number of the exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please put the photograph the right way so that we can see it on the ELMO. First put a circle around your own house and mark it with number 1?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: This is my house (marks).

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Put number 1 next to it, then tell us what you're putting circles around, your neighbours' houses, and say, "This is the house of such and such a person," and then the next house, mark the next house, number 2.

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: This is Josip Kupreskic's house (marks).

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: That's number 2; right?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: On the other side from my house is Zoran Kupreskic's house (marks).

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Then mark that with a number 3?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Then Mirjan Kupreskic's house and his father's house (marks).

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mark that with the number 4.

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: (Marks). Up here is the house of Enver Sahic. He's a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mark that with a number 5.

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: (Marks). Then Alaman's house is number 6 (marks).

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Six.

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Now Sakib Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: This is Sakib Ahmic (marks).

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Number 7?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: And then Vlatko's house (marks).

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Vlatko's house is number 8. So I don't think we need the other houses. So now we have completed the marking. Now, tell me, often during this trial the names of Ivica and Ivo Kupreskic were mentioned often. Is this one person or are these two persons?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: No, these are two persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Who is Ivo Kupreskic and who is Ivica Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Ivica Kupreskic is the son of Ivo Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So Ivo Kupreskic is your father-in-law; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me now, your husband is related to Zoran Kupreskic; right? And, of course, he is related the same way to Mirjan Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Mirjan and Zoran -- or rather, Mirjan's and Zoran's father and Ivo Kupreskic's father are brothers.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So they are cousins; right?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: When you came to live in the village of Pirici, and it's mentioned as Ahmici most of time, did you see the house of Sakib Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. You can see it very well from my house, Sakib's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I started the wrong way. I started this question the wrong way. Can you describe the appearance of this house?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. That is an older house. That is to say, the lower part is -- I mean, it's not a multi-storied building. There are rooms, and there's an upper part. It's a very old house.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, could you see, from your house, the entrance to the lower part of that house?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes, you can see it very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: All right. So then you can see the entrance, right?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Sakib Ahmic had a divorce?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I heard that he was not living with his wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Can you say approximately when this happened?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I don't know. No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see something from Sakib Ahmic's house, on the basis of which one could conclude that for a certain period of time Sakib Ahmic lived in the basement of his house?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Very often we would see him in the garden sitting, walking. He would sit most of the time, alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: In what part?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: In the lower part of the house, in front of the lower part of the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Can you say for how long this kind of a situation lasted?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Until I went to Germany, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: The day you came back from Germany, where did he live then? Do you know or do you not know?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Since we've been speaking about kinship, could you tell me how are Branko and Josip Kupreskic related to your husband, because their houses are there too, if I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So who is Branko Kupreskic? How is he related to him?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: He is his brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: And Josip Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Josip Kupreskic is also his brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: And tell me, did Ivica have any brothers, at that time, who worked in Germany, or any other kind of kinsmen?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Ivica had a brother called Branko Kupreskic who lived in Germany, and who has been there for the past 17 years, and who had opened a restaurant. And another brother, in 1992, in mid-February, went there. That's Josip. He went to work as a cook for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What about yourself, did you go to Germany at some point in time?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: When did you go?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I went, my husband, my three children, and I and also two children of my brother's -- or of my husband's brother, Josip, went there. We went to stay with Branko.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: When was this?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: On the 30th of March, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Court why you went together, all together, why you all went to Germany?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: We went because of the Serb aggression towards Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, in Germany, did you stay in Germany on a tourist visa. Was this a tourist visit or did you legalise your stay in Germany?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I went there and I was listed as a refugee, and I got that kind of a visa.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask the usher to hand these documents out.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D12/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: You've just had a look at this document. So could you tell me please if this is a photocopy of your passport?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. This is my passport, a photocopy.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Now, please look at the part where the German visas are, and could you explain for how long these visas were valid?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters please have a copy on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: My last reporting was supposed to have taken place on the 13th of March, 1993, and that is when I was supposed to go there for an extension of this duldung visa, which is exactly what I did. On the 13th I extended it, although I said that I was going home. They didn't want to interrupt this duldung visa because we were under their control, under their supervision, and they didn't want to take any responsibility for our departure to Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what this visa means, the one you mentioned? What kind of visa is this?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: It is the duldung visa. It gives you refugee status.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did this status give you any material security in the Federal Republic of Germany?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What did this consist of, this material security?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Well, when we went to get this duldung visa at the appropriate office, we went to the social security people, and then on the basis of this duldung visa we got social security every month.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did your husband go back to Vitez at the same time when you did or at a different point in time?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: No. My husband took a plane back on the 13th of March, 1993. He took a return ticket. Our car was with me. Ivica came there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: All right. But what did you say? You first said that you (sic) went there with you?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Now I am asking you what --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel is overlapping the witness.

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: He first returned in mid-June. Ivica returned in mid-June with cars full of humanitarian aid for Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, why did he return on his own without you and the children?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Well, he returned because certain persons threatened to blow up our house.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Why was that?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Because he was supposed to be where everybody was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall the exact date when he returned on his own?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: The 13th of June, 1992. That was first time that he returned on his own.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: When did your children return?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: The children returned with my husband. My husband took an aeroplane on the 13th of March, 1993, he came on plane, and then we agreed that the children and I could not stay on there anymore, and that they missed their home and their father, and that they were fed up, generally speaking, and we thought that there weren't any problems in Vitez, as there weren't, that his company was still working, and we agreed that Ivica should go back with the car that I had already with me in Germany, and that I'd take care of this duldung visa on the 13th of March, 1993, and that I take a return ticket and go back to stay with my husband Ivica.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: When you agreed that you and the children, separately, in all fairness, returned to Vitez, did your husband tell you that this was dangerous for any reason?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: No, no, he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What did he tell you then? How would he describe the situation in Vitez then?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: He said that it was normal, that the children were going to school, the people were going to work, that our company was working normally.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So if I understood you correctly, when your husband visited on the 13th of April, 1993, he did not tell you in any way that he knew of any kind of imminent threat or danger?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: On the contrary. I think that he told you that the situation was peaceful and that you could come back. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Now, you left Germany in which way? Which means of transportation did you take? On what date, on what airline?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I left Germany on the 14th of April, 1993. My brother-in-law, Branko Kupreskic, took me to the airport in Dusseldorf, by car. I was going back, and I had a return ticket of my husband, Ivica, and the plane left at 6.00 p.m., and we flew to Zagreb and Split. I arrived in Split at around 9.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: And tell me, when you came to Split did somebody meet you there or did you set out for Vitez on your own?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I was met by my husband, Ivica, and by Vlatko Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: After having said hello to him, of course, how did you continue your voyage? Did you go straight to Vitez or did you stop at some point?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: They came in a Yugo 45 passenger car, and we left the airport and went to Baska Voda.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. You said a Yugo 45. What's a Yugo 45?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: It's a car.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: It's the make of a car; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: All right. It's important to say what this is because it's not really a famous car, so it's not that everybody in the courtroom has to know about it. I apologise for interrupting and please continue.

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: We took the car and went to Baska Voda, and then we spent the night at Vladislav Simic's place.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Who spent the night at Mr. Simic's please?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I did; my husband, Ivica; and Vlatko Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Then what happened?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Well, we sat there, we had some coffee, we chatted, and then we went to bed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: When did you continue your journey?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Around 6.00. We packed our things and went to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me which road you took to Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Vrgorac, Capljina, Tomislavgrad, Vran, Sebesic, Opara, Novi Travnik, Vitez and then we came home.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: On the way did you have any unpleasantness?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. At Sebesici we were stopped by soldiers and they didn't let's us pass. We said we were going home, and I said that I had been in Germany and that I have three children at home, and they said that they didn't want to be held responsible for us if anything happened to us. Then we continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me the discussion with the soldiers that stopped you. Did you talk to them or your husband?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: No. My husband talked to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if I understood you correctly, then he would be able to give more detail of that talk than you?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: The towns you enumerated, will you tell us which towns are in Croatia, which are in Bosnia, and which are in Herzegovina, if any of them are there?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: You told us the route you took to Vitez, and you enumerated certain towns. Would you try and tell us a bit about geography and tell us which of these towns are in Croatia, which are in Herzegovina, and which are in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Well, Baska Voda, where we spent the night, is in Croatia. We went by Vrgorac.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: And where is Vrgorac?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: It is in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Then we crossed into Bosnia-Herzegovina, went to Capljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Capljina is a part called Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Then we continued on towards Tomislavgrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Where is Tomislavgrad?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: That's also Herzegovina. Then we continued our journey to Vran, Vran-Planina, Mount Vran. It was a macadamised road surface. There was a lot of mud and it was a very unpleasant drive, but we, nonetheless, continued our journey and went across Vrana and then down to Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: That is Bosnia; is it not?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes it is Bosnia. Across Vakuf, Sebesic to Novi Travnik and Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us did you take the shortest route from Split to Vitez or is this a longer route?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Well, this is longer than the normal route, and it is a byroad.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Can you give us a comparison? Is it double the route going that way? Or --

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think, more than double. Over 400 kilometres if you take that route, the route we took.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Otherwise how far is it?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Vitez/Split is about 210 kilometres going the more direct route.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did your husband explain to you why you were using this by-route?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: No, he did not ask me and he didn't explain why.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Now you arrived in Vitez. What was the date that you arrived in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I arrived in Vitez on the 15th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: At what time?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: At 6:30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: When you arrived in Vitez, where did you go first?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I first went, quite normally, to my house, and we took our luggage out there. I said hello to Ivica's father, to my aunt, to my children and with Gordana Vidovic as well. She had come to get some water for just a minute because they had no water and so she came to get some water and returned home.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me what about your mother. Did you go to visit your mother?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We just unloaded our luggage and I said hello to my children and my mother-in-law and then we went to my mother's house. They knew that I was coming. There were my two brothers there, two sisters there, and their children were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: How many brothers have you got?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I had three brothers.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: At that time you had three brothers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: How come only two of your brothers greeted you?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: When I came we had a cup of coffee to drink, and I said, "Where's Karlo?"

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: You mean your third brother?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Karlo is my third brother. They couldn't tell me where he was. It was only later, when I returned home, that the telephone rang, and it was my brother Karlo ringing up. I asked him why he wasn't in the house, because he knew that I was coming, and he said, "Doesn't matter, sister. We'll see each other tomorrow." I was at the 2S (phoen) cafe, owned by a Muslim named Osman, and it is in a part of Vitez known as the Mahala.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: That is the Muslim part, is it not?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is a Muslim cafe. That is to say the owner of the 2S cafe is a Muslim by the name of Osman, and he was in the cafe with friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: The next day, did you see Karlo? And what was the fate of your brother? Could you tell the Court about that? I know it is very difficult for you. He was your youngest brother, was he not?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was my youngest brother. While we talked, he said, "There's no problem, sis, we'll see each other tomorrow." But that never came to pass. It never happened because my brother, on the fourth day, that is to say the 19th of March, no, the 19th of April; I beg your pardon. On the 19th of April, he lost his life when a shell hit and some of the shrapnel hit him here (indicating), in this part of the brain. He was wounded and that's where it lodged. That's what happened. My oldest brother transported him to Vitez, to the emergency centre there. He spent the entire night there because they were not able to transport him to Travnik because there was shooting. The next day, in the morning, Karlo was transported to Travnik by UNPROFOR. He spent two days lying in Travnik in a coma. They didn't do anything to him. Two days later, UNPROFOR transported Karlo to Zenica. In Zenica, he was lying in bed in Zenica for a few days and was operated by Ivo Blajic several days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: The doctor was a Croat, was he not?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes. His name was Ivo Blajic. All the telephone conversations were between the Zenica hospital and the ambulance service in Vitez. Several days after Karlo's operation, Ivo Blajic, Dr. Ivo Blajic, called and said that it was not a good idea for Karlo to stay in the hospital because somebody could enter his room and take away the apparatus that had been tied to him, that it wasn't a good idea for him to stay there. UNPROFOR once again took Karlo from the Zenica hospital and transferred him to Split, in Croatia. I beg your pardon. Karlo was in Split until the 8th of June, when he died. He died on the 49th day. He was in a refrigerator for two weeks because the town of Split did not allow him to be buried at the Lovrinac cemetery. It was impossible for him to be transported, his body to be transported to Vitez, because the Lasva Valley and the town of Vitez were in a total encirclement by the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So when did you bury him, ultimately?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Two weeks later.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I mean in Vitez, when did you bury him in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Can I say what I want to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead. I apologise for interrupting?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Two weeks later, Karlo was buried in Tomislavgrad. That was where he was. He was buried in the presence of several locals, and a clergy man. His mother wasn't there, his sisters and brothers weren't there. Last year, that is to say 1998, at the beginning of April, we transferred Karlo's body to Vitez and let me just add that we didn't know where Karlo was buried until after the war, until Karlo Vrebac from Vitez came and he was in Split at the time, and that's when we learned where Karlo had been buried. In the summer of 1994, we started out to Split to find our brother's burial site.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Let us go back to the 15th of April when you returned to Vitez. So you visited your mother and your brothers, and I suppose you went back to your house after that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So we can carry on with events in your own house, but before you continue to tell us about that, can you continue, do you need a little time to recover?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes, you can continue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Before I ask you what happened in your own house, I'm going to ask you about a Bosnian custom that you have, the customs in Bosnia. Before a friend comes to visit a friend, or a godfather, or a cousin, is it usual to ring up first and say, can I come and visit you today say at 2205 hundred hours or can you come any time and your welcome with open arms?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: No. Nobody has to ring up. You can come in any time. Everybody is welcome at all times, and is always made to feel welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So you don't have to be announced earlier?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: No, you don't answer --

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Just to clear up the differences in certain cultures and customs. Now you can go on to tell us who visited you and what happened in your own house after you had settled in on the 15th of April.

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I spent very little time at my mother's place and I went back to my own house where I found Mirko Sakic, and Miroslav Pudza. Then three refugees came, Marica Manda, and their mother-in-law Luca. So people would turn up and leave. They were not all there at the same time. One batch of people would arrive, others would leave. There would be a general coming and going. Zoran Kupreskic and his wife Mira turned up for a very brief visit just to say hello and then they went straight back home because they had guests at their own house.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did they tell you who was at their house?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Gordana Vidovic had come visiting to their place. Then Mirjan Kupreskic arrived with his wife, Ljubica. There was Miroslav Pudza, Mira Vidovic, Franjo's boy; Ljubica Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic's wife. Vlatko wasn't there because we had come together. There was Vlatko's mother, Marica, and also Mirjan's and Zoran's mother. She was there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So that would be more or less who was there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Now, why is this important? It is important for you to enumerate all these people because it is that, one of the witnesses talked about people who were in your house and enumerated only men, so one would have concluded that only men had come to visit your house.

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Well, there were more men, but they had come to joke with my husband and said, "Well, we've come to see you," because he was recently married.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did you serve your guests anything?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I made some coffee. I offered them some drink and little assortments to go with the drinks.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What did you discuss on the occasion? Were you in the room all the time? Tell us the topics you discussed.

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Well, generally they asked me what it was like in Germany, and because most of the people that were there had never been to Germany. They asked me what was life like in Germany, and how Branko's children were, and how my husband and I were finding life there, and so on. I asked them what had been going on in my absence. So for the most part, that was what we discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Were they interested in your journey from Split to Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes, this interested them a great deal about how we had arrived because, already at that time, there were some checkpoints along the way, especially Vran-Planina, Mt. Vran. That is to say, very rarely did people go that way, take that route. So we talked about our journey home.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell us, please, when did you go to bed, approximately? What time?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: The guests dispersed at about midnight. I cleared up, I washed the dishes, I had a shower, I went to bed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: How did you wake up, and why? What was that like, your waking moments?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: In the morning, a little after 4.00 a.m., I was woken up by my husband, Ivica. He said that something was wrong, and that I should get up. I said that I didn't want to get up, that I hadn't had enough sleep, and that I had just come to my own bed after a year's absence and that I wanted to go on sleeping. He shouted at me and said that I had to get up to get the children ready, to get myself ready, to get some things together, and that we had to escape from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did he explain why?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't. He didn't say why. He told me that something was wrong, and that we had to go to a shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What did you do then?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Well, I got up, I woke the children, we got ready, I took some clothes with us and some food, packed some clothes and food, and we left to the shelter a little before 5.00 a.m. It was about 5 to 5.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Which shelter did you, in fact, go to?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: We went to the shelter at Drevceva's (phoen) houses. It's the shelter belonging to Dragan and Jelena Trajanovski. That's where the shelter was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I should now like to ask the usher's assistance to hand out the next document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D13/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: One more I know, but I need -- I shall give after my questions. Sorry. Yes, I have. I have, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Now please have a look at this photo file, and could you please describe what you see on picture number 1.

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Picture number 1, I see the house where Dragan and Jelina Trajanovski's shelter is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: You are one of the very few persons using the word "Trajanovski." I imagine that he is a Macedonian, judging by his last name; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: You're actually talking about Jozo Vrebac's house, are you?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Jozo Vrebac or Jelina. Jelina is the daughter of Jozo Vrebac, and she got married to Dragan Trajanovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: All right. So it's the same building when we're talking about the Trajanovskis' shelter. It is actually the same building that people who say that it's the Vrebacs' shelter. So we're trying to clarify this so that we know that it's not two different shelters but one. Please look at photograph number 2. Please describe picture number 2.

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: At the entrance. This is the main door. The entrance to the house. On the right-hand side you go down into the shelter, to the basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether this basement was underground or what did it look like?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was underground, and there was perhaps, I don't know, half a metre was above the ground and all the rest was underground, and I know that because of two small windows that were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please describe photograph number 3?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: This is the very entrance now, the very entrance into the shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Picture number 4?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: This is the shelter. This is the area that we were in.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Picture number 5.

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: The same thing. The same. The same area that we were in, where there was a bed, a mattress, where the few elderly and sickly people could lie and rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Now, picture number 6, please.

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: The same, the same shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Picture number 7?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: The same thing. It's the shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Since this photo file was made much later, I mean, after you were there, can you tell me, on the basis of what you remember about this area and what you've just seen on the photographs, whether there have been any changes made in the meantime, or was it the same in this basement?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Well, these sofas weren't there. There weren't any beds. There was just one mattress that was on the floor. Not these mattresses and sofas that we saw here. It wasn't there when we were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any other changes?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many rooms there were altogether downstairs in that basement?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I didn't really look. I was in this main room where we all were, and also, there was a small niche where there was a mattress, where the elderly people would take turns so they could lie down.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So there was more than one room?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know. I just know about this one room. It was dark, there was no electricity.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: When you came to this shelter, were there any people there already? Were there a lot of people there?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: No. There weren't a lot of people there. There was only a few because I was one of the first to arrive. My three sons and I were among the first to arrive.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did your husband go with you?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes. My husband went with me up to the house of Ivica Vidovic, nicknamed Jevco.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: And then?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: And then Ivica came back to wake up these refugees, Marica Manda and their mother-in-law Luca.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know their last name?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Didak.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: They were refugees from where?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: From the village of Didaci above Turbe. They lived in Branko Kupreskic's house, the brother of Ivica, and he lived in Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So now you reached the shelter. Could you tell me who else came to this shelter, and in which order, if you remember this, because nobody asked you to tell us anything that you don't remember.

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I remember. When I arrived, there were a few people there, a few women and children. Very shortly afterwards Mirjan Kupreskic arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Alone or with someone?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: In a wheelbarrow he had his mother-in-law. His wife, Ljubica Kupreskic was walking behind him, carrying two small children.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Just a minute. Did any of them remain in this shelter that you were in?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Ljubica Kupreskic with her two children and her mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: They remained in this same shelter?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes. They remained in this same shelter, and they put her mother on that mattress in that niche that was there. She was very sick. She couldn't walk.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was the time when you first arrived in that shelter?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Well, ten past five, quarter pass five, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately when Mirjan arrived with his wife and children?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Mirjan arrived soon after I did. This was approximately five or ten minutes later.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Five or ten minutes; right?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes, five to ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me whether any other acquaintances of yours came to the basement?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Gordana Vidovic came; her mother, Milka Vidovic; Dragica Omazic with her two children. Then Andza Livancic, her husband Marko Livancic; Ivo Vidovic; Mila Vidovic; Nevenka Marijanovic with three children; Brankica Papic with two children.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: All of them were in this one same room that you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me approximately how big that room was? Could you perhaps express this in square metres?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: It was a small room. It wasn't big.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Can you give us a rough estimate or not?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I can't. I can't. It wasn't big. No, no, I can't really tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: At the time when you came to this room, was there any reason for you to be terrified by anything you heard or saw?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. There was a lot of shooting and there were strong detonations.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: When you arrived?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand what you asked me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Listen to me carefully. I'm asking you -- well, okay. You mentioned shootings and detonation, but as you were walking along the road from your house to Jozo Vrebac's house, did the shooting start already then?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: When you were in the shelter did the shooting start then?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Now, how did these people who sought shelter react to the sound of shooting?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: How did the people in that shelter react when they heard shooting outside?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: It was awful. There were only a few men there. It was all women, children, and old people. It was dreadful. The women were panicked, and the children were crying, naturally.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did you receive any information within the shelter as to what was going on outside the shelter?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: No. No, I did not have any information.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did you talk about it as to what it might have been or was it just guesswork?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Well, it was guesswork. At that moment, we were so frightened and we were so terrified. We all turned to our children to pacify them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Then tell me, how long did you stay in this shelter?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I was in that shelter until the 17th of April, 1993, in the evening, until about 6.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Then when did you leave this shelter and where did you go to?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Then they told us that the Muslims, the Mujahedeen, had barged into Krtina-Mahala, and many women and children down there were running. They were crying and screaming, and they were barefoot and they hardly had any clothes on. They ran up to us, and all these people who ran out of Krtina-Mahala were evacuated to Donja Rovna.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So you were there until the evening of the second day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So now let's go back to the events in this shelter at Jozo Vrebac's place. It's easier for me to also call it "Jozo Vrebac's place," so we're going to call the shelter that from now on. Did your husband, Ivica, show up during the day at this shelter?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did. Ivica came sometime in the afternoon on the 16th. He brought in food. He brought in food for me and the children.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Only for you or for others?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Well, to all of us, of course. We didn't eat it on our own. We shared the food.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did he come only once or did he come a few more times?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes, he came in the evening too with Ivica and Mirjan Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, since you mentioned that Mirjan came too, do you remember how many times he came, and can you tell us the time when he came?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: He came when Ivica brought us lunch. That was in the afternoon, around 2.00. And Mirjan was with Ivica, and also in the evening they came.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did Zoran come too?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Zoran did too, and Mirko Sakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did Zoran come alone or with Mirjan? I mean, did Mirjan and Zoran come separately or together, or do you not simply recall?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: On one occasion they came together, both Mirjan and Zoran, and Mirko Sakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, when Mirjan came to this shelter, why did he come?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: He came to bring food to his wife as well. Then his son Marko, who was very young at the time, he was just over a year old, he was ill, he had a high fever, and he came to see his son, to see his wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, why did Zoran come?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Well, Zoran came also to see us, and Zoran's wife was -- well, we were nearby. She was in Milutin Vidovic's house. So he went to see Mira Kupreskic at Milutin's, and then he would continue and see us because it wasn't far away.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what is the distance between the Vrebac shelter and Milutin Vidovic's shelter, I mean, as the crow flies?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe this would be a good time to take a break, and then we can continue after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. So we will take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: --- Upon resuming at 12.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: May we continue?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us whether you know what shelter the parents of Zoran and Mirjan were in.

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: They were in the shelter I was in.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Would you try and enumerate all the people who were with you, but slowly, please, so that -- for the purposes of the record.

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Vlatko Kupreskic was there, with his wife and two children and his mother. Ljubica Kupreskic was there, Mirjan Kupreskic's wife, with her two children and her mother. I was there with my three children. Gordana Vidovic and her mother. Dragica Omazic, with her two children. Marko Livancic, Landza Livancic, Anto Vidovic, Jela Vidovic, Slavica Vidovic, Ivo Vidovic, Milan Vidovic; Nevenka Marjanovic, with her three children; Papic Brankica, with two children; and Papic Lucija, with her five children. Then there was Marko Santic, Lucka Santic, Zeljka Santic, with one child; Gordana Santic, with two children; Nevenka Santic, with two children; Lucija Santic, also with two children; Ana Santic; Jozo Vrebac; and Andja Vrebac.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: That would be all?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: When you saw Mirjan Kupreskic on that day, do you remember what he was wearing, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Mirjan Santic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm asking about Mirjan Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Mirjan Kupreskic; I beg your pardon. Mirjan Kupreskic was wearing a sort of brown jacket, and he had some long socks, woollen socks. That was particularly noticeable.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean civilian clothing, or military?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: No, he had civilian clothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what Zoran was wearing?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Zoran had civilian pants and a camouflage jacket.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: On that first day, the day you went to the shelter and heard the shooting --

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that whole day was terrible.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: -- could you assess where the shooting was coming from? If you could, you could. If you couldn't, you couldn't.

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: In the shelter we were not able to say where it was coming from. All we heard was loud shots and detonation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, was there shooting on the second day?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was shooting on the second day as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Can you, on this map of Ahmici, show us the route you took when you went to Rovna on the second day?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, then, please do so.

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: This is the shelter, the house I was in (indicating). Then we went along this route. That was a local road. Then we got up on to the main road here (indicating), went left, and once again went right, on to a local road, towards Donja Rovna. Across the old railway line, across Lasva -- Radak's Bridge. That's where I went, to Pero Santic's place.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You can sit down again. Did anybody else of your family go to Pero Santic's house, your broader family?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes. While we were going along that road, my children, my eldest son, Dragan, who was 14 at the time, carried his seven-year-old brother. I led my father-in-law, who was very ill. He was born in 1925. My middle son had with him -- was carrying some food and clothing. My 14-year-old son was crying. He called Ljubica Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic's wife. He called out to her because she had two small children and an ill mother that she was taking in a wheelbarrow. We were not able to hear or see one another. Dragan was crying. We came to Pero Santic's house, and my eldest son, the 14-year-old, was crying, and then he returned under the hail of gunfire. He went back to look for Ljubica Kupreskic, Mirjan's wife. He found them amongst the mass of people. He took her mother, which she had been taking in a wheelbarrow, and brought her there, then went back again to help her with the children because, as I've already said, the little boy, Marko, who was a little over 1, was very ill at the time. So he came back to Pero Santic's house with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Rovna?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I stayed about ten days.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: When you returned, which route -- where did you go to?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: From Rovna, I went to Kristo Niko's place. I spent several days there. I was not able to stay there any longer, so I returned to my own house after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: This house there, your house?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: While you were in the shelters, did you know what was happening around you? Or did you know nothing except for hearing the shooting?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Well, we guessed at what was going on, but we didn't actually know. We just heard the strong detonations and shooting and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: When you went to Rovna, did you know what had happened after you had left? That is, who remained after you? Did you know them?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have completed my questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Counsel Radovic. I wonder whether there is any cross-examination by other Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, none of the other counsel intends asking any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Terrier?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Madam. My name is Franck Terrier. I'm one of the Prosecution attorneys. As you were told, I'm going to ask you some questions following your testimony. You described to us your family, and you told us that you have three sons. I believe that you said that the oldest one was 14 years old at that time, that is, 1993; that one of the other of your children was 7 years old. How old was the third one?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: The third child was 13 years old. My middle son was 13 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you describe to us what your relationship was until you left Germany, that is, in March of 1992 -- your relationship with your Muslim neighbours? Specifically, the ones that you mentioned, the ones whose names you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: We had very good relations. We even visited one another from time to time. We never had any problems, any disputes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: For instance, so that we can have a clear idea, did you have these Muslim neighbours come to your house? That is, you and your husband. Did either of you go to them?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did, and they would come to us. We would go to them. We even had Muslim godfathers for our two sons, Dragan and Josip. Dragan is a godfather to Varupa Vahid, and the middle son, Josip, the godfather is Rasim Gradinovic, our neighbour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: However, unless I'm wrong, when you came home on the 15th of April, 1993, not a single one of them came to your house.

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: They didn't have occasion to because we came late. When I came, that is to say, I stayed there for a very little time and then went to my mother's, and it was already late, so they didn't come then.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: But the fact that they didn't come to see you, can we say that the reason for that is that they didn't have the occasion to? Or was it that the nature of your relationships, the relationship between the communities, had changed, and that these kinds of visits could no longer take place?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know. I couldn't answer that question. I don't know. I really don't know why nobody came to visit us, to see me and my children.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Before you left for Germany, did you have any type of professional activity that you performed?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter couldn't hear "Yes" or "No."

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what that job was?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I am head of an independent catering shop called Grill Ivica, and it was a meeting place. Everybody came there, Muslims and Croats and Serbs. There was no difference. Up until -- that is for as long as I was there. Afterwards, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I didn't understand exactly where that restaurant was.

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: It was in a street called -- it was in Vitez. It was in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: What was the name of the restaurant?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Grill Ivica. Grill Ivica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Who was the owner?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: The proprietor was my husband at the time, Ivica Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Where in Vitez was that restaurant?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: It was in Petar Svacic Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I have to admit that I don't know where that street in Vitez is, but could you explain where, in relation to the Hotel Vitez, where the restaurant was, that is in relation to the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: From the hotel you take the main road. From the main road from the hotel, on the main road it is about 500 metres, and then from the main road you go into town. It's another, perhaps, 300 to 400 metres. You go straight, and at the corner there is the chemist's, the pharmacy on the left-hand side. You go left, and some 50 metres from that pharmacist on the right-hand side is where Grill Ivica is located.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: When you left for Germany in March of 1992, what happened to the restaurant?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: At the time, the restaurant was taken over by my brother, Ivo Grabovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: But your husband remained the owner; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: No. My brother stayed to work there in the restaurant, Ivo Grabovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: But who became or who was the owner after March 1992?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: In 1992, in March, when we left for Germany, the owner was my brother, Ivo Grabovac. He stayed on as the owner.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: All right. I understand. You told us that you had gone to Germany because of the fact that it was not safe in the area of Vitez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: No. My husband and I and our children left because of the Serbian aggression on Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Perhaps we didn't understand one another, but, in fact, it was a question of a lack of security which led you to take that decision, that is, you wanted to be sure that your family would be safe by going to Germany?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: In Vitez, there were no problems in Vitez. Nothing could be felt in Vitez then, but we left because of the Serbian aggression on Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you specify where in Germany you went?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: We went to Essen, to an apartment, to the apartment of Ivica's brother, Branko. Branko, at the time, perhaps in mid-February, Branko went to Herne where he took a restaurant. He lived and worked there, and he left me and my children his apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did you have a job in Germany?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't work.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: How did you live? What were your resources?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I lived from the social security that I received.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: As regards this assistance that was given to you by the German authorities, can you tell us what your status was? You said that you were a refugee?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: That is pursuant to the Geneva Convention?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You were permitted to stay in Germany as a result of that convention; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I got a duldung visa and refugee status.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Excuse me, I don't know German law that well in this respect. When one gets a refugee status, it seems to me that one is not allowed to leave the country that has taken you in.

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Nobody made me leave the country. However, they did not want to interrupt this duldung visa of mine because they were held responsible for us. They guaranteed our security.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: According to the copy of your passport, it seems that the deadline, the last date where you were allowed to remain in Germany, had been set as the 13th of April, 1993, and that, in fact, you couldn't stay in Germany beyond that date?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I could have, and it says there that they extended it for six months. I did not go to extend the duldung visa all the time. The longer I stayed, the longer they extended it. Sometimes they extended it for six months, sometimes four months or six months, et cetera. Then on the 13th, on the 13th of April, when I went, they extended it for another six months.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Therefore, when you had taken your decision to go back to your home in Bosnia, it was a voluntary decision that you had taken?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, a voluntary decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You could have extended your stay in Germany?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I could have.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: If you had taken that decision, it's that it seemed to you that there was no problem of safety in Vitez or in the region at that date, in the area, for you and your family?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes, because my husband said that everything was normal in Vitez, that it was peaceful and quiet, that children were going to school and people were going to work and that there was no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Therefore, it seemed to you that in respect of April of 1992, when the Serbian threat prompted you to leave Bosnia, in respect of that date, the situation had improved?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I left on the 30th of March, 1992. I went to Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I understood that, but what I was asking you is that you decided to leave, in March of 1992, for Germany because the situation seemed threatening to you, and you decided, in April 1993, to return because the situation no longer seemed to be problematic for you, so, therefore, one would think that in your mind, the situation had improved. Between March of 1992 and April of 1993, the situation in that region of Central Bosnia had improved, from your point of view and from the point of you view of your husband; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: In 1992, in March, I left because of the Serb aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina. My husband and I, in 1994 (sic), decided that I should come back, that there were no problems in Vitez, the children were going to school, that people were going to work normally, and that there was a normal life and that there were no problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: All right. You told us that you left Germany on the 14th of April, 1993 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Excuse me. The interpreter said that the interpreter mentioned 1994. Perhaps you meant 1993. That was the French -- you came back in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes. The correction was made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I was listening to the French too, and in French it said that the witness did say 1994. Therefore, I'm asking the witness whether she did, in fact, mean 1993, that is the year that you decided to go back to Vitez. It was 1993, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise if I said that. I returned in 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You told us, Madam, that you left Germany on the 14th of April, 1993, and that you were living in Essen and that you had taken the plane at Dusseldorf. What is the distance between those two cities?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Between Essen and Dusseldorf -- or rather, when my husband had left, I already went to Herne to stay with Ivica brother's, Branko, and then from Herne to Dusseldorf it's about 30-odd kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You told us that you took the plane in Dusseldorf around 6.00 in the afternoon for Zagreb. Do you remember what airline you used?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I went back using my husband's return plane ticket. At 18.00 hours, the plane took off from Dusseldorf and went to Zagreb, and then from Zagreb to Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: What airline did you use?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Croatia Airlines.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: In order to take this trip from Germany to Croatia at that point, did you need to have a visa, an administrative visa either from the German or Croatian authorities because I understand that you did not have a Croatian passport at that point.

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't need any kind of visa.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You told us that you changed planes in Zagreb, and that you took another plane for Split and that you arrived at 9.30 in the evening. What airline did you take in order to go from Split to Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You told us that when you arrived at the Split airport, Ivica and Vlatko Kupreskic were waiting for you. Weren't you a little bit surprised to see Vlatko Kupreskic there?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I was not surprised.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Do you know what your husband's professional work is, aside from the hospital -- excuse me, the restaurant that you spoke about a little while ago?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: It's the restaurant, the sale of food and alcoholic and non-alcoholic beverages. In addition to that, my husband has a privately owned company.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Leaving aside the restaurant, let's speak about this private company. What do you know about it?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: It was a privately owned company. Mostly it was food, alcoholic and non-alcoholic beverages, and meat products, cured meat products.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did Ivica, your husband, and Vlatko Kupreskic, did they make the trip from Vitez to Split to come get you at the airport, or as far as you know, was there another reason for their having made that trip?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes, they came to pick me up, and also en route, they collected some goods.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You mean that the trip to Split also had as its objective an order to pick up a delivery of merchandise?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Primarily, my arrival, and in addition to that, they could also collect some merchandise for their company.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Were you there when they picked up the merchandise?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: No. No. No, I was not there. They took it as they were coming to pick me up. They first took over this merchandise and then they picked me up.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Before they came to get you; I see. What kind of luggage did you have with you?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't have much luggage because Ivica left by car with the children on the 9th of April, so I sent all my luggage with Ivica, so I only had my own bag and perhaps another smaller bag.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You told us that your husband and Vlatko Kupreskic came to get you in a Yugo 45. To whom did that car belong?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: That was my car.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did your husband have another car?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes, he had a Mercedes 240D.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could one say that the Yugo 45 was a very little car?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Why didn't your husband take the Mercedes with him?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Because the road across Mt. Vran is in poor condition. It is not an asphalt road. It is a muddy road, a very bad road.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You mean that the Yugo 45 would be a better car under those conditions than the Mercedes?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: What colour is that Yugo?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: A mousy colour, grey, sort of bluish-grey.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: What colour is the Mercedes that belonged to your husband?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Dark green.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: May I ask the usher to put Prosecution Document 32 on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I'm showing you that photograph, but it's not about the house, but rather for the car that's behind, that's near the garage. Could you confirm to us that that's the Yugo 45?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That is a Yugo 45 owned by Vlatko Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: But to the left on this picture -- that was taken, of course, long after the period that we're interested in -- we see a Mercedes. Who did that car belong to, as far as you know? On the left side of the photograph, you can see that there's a Mercedes there.

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Vlatko Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: As far as you know, when did he acquire that Mercedes, the one that we see on the left side?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: That Mercedes? Vlatko Kupreskic bought it from my husband. I could not exactly tell when. I could not tell for sure. I know that my husband brought this car in from Germany and Ivica sold that car to Vlatko.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: When? At what time did your husband import that car from Germany?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I can't say. I couldn't explain exactly, because after the war, my husband and I often travelled to Germany, went there and went back, and we bought quite a few cars in the process. So I could not really remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You mean that your husband bought a lot of cars in Germany so he could sell them or resell them in Bosnia; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: No, no. No, I meant that we bought a kombi van for ourselves, and then we got a jeep, and then we got a refrigerator truck, and it was all for our own needs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Whatever the case may be, the Mercedes that we see in the photograph, to the left of the house, is not the Mercedes that your husband had in 1993; more specifically in April 1993. It's rather, a car that was imported after the war?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. This is Vlatko's Mercedes and our Mercedes is green.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: However, in April 1993, your husband and Vlatko Kupreskic, in order to make the trip between Vitez and Split in April 1993, preferred to use the Yugo 45 than the Mercedes that your husband had and you explained why to us. My question is: What type of merchandise were put into that car before your husband and Vlatko Kupreskic came to get you at the airport?

utterances.speaker: ANKICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know because they took the merchandise before picking me up. I didn't see it. I don't know what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
